options: Wraps a QNode so it behaves like a standard torch.nn.Module layer, accepting and returning tensors and participating fully in PyTorch's autograd system
Converts a PyTorch model entirely into a quantum circuit with no classical layers remaining
Only works for TensorFlow, despite its name
Replaces PennyLane's parameter-shift rule with classical backpropagation through the physical circuit
questions.explain: TorchLayer makes a QNode behave exactly like any other PyTorch layer -- accepting tensor inputs, returning tensor outputs, and correctly computing gradients when .backward() is called, using parameter-shift under the hood.

questions.q: In the concrete hybrid architecture described (classical layer -> quantum layer -> classical layer), what role does the quantum layer typically play?
options: A small quantum 'core' sandwiched between classical pre- and post-processing layers, not an all-quantum model end to end
It replaces every classical layer entirely, with no classical computation anywhere in the model
It only runs during inference, never during training
It computes the final output directly with no further classical processing
questions.explain: The realistic shape of most hybrid QML models is a small quantum core between classical dimensionality-reduction and classical post-processing layers, trained end-to-end with ordinary backprop outside the quantum layer and parameter-shift inside it.

questions.q: How does TorchLayer make the quantum layer's gradient available to PyTorch's autograd system during the backward pass?
options: It internally runs PennyLane's parameter-shift gradient computation and returns that result to autograd as if it had come from ordinary backpropagation -- autograd doesn't need to know the underlying method differed
It requires the user to manually compute and inject the gradient at every training step
It disables autograd entirely for any model containing a quantum layer
It converts the quantum circuit into a lookup table computed once before training begins
questions.explain: TorchLayer handles the parameter-shift computation internally and hands the result back to autograd in the expected format, which is exactly what makes dropping a QNode into a PyTorch model work seamlessly without hand-written hybrid-loop code.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a real practical integration gotcha when combining PennyLane circuits with PyTorch models?
options: Data type mismatches (e.g., PennyLane expecting float64 vs. PyTorch's default float32), and quantum devices not natively vectorizing over a batch dimension the way GPU operations do
PennyLane circuits can never be combined with any classical layer under any circumstances
PyTorch does not support any form of automatic differentiation
TorchLayer only works with exactly one qubit, never more
questions.explain: Dtype mismatches throw type errors, and unsupported devices can silently fall back to looping over batch samples one at a time (correct but slow) -- both genuine, documented gotchas when integrating PennyLane circuits into PyTorch models.

questions.q: What would break, practically, if PennyLane instead required manually intercepting the backward pass every time a quantum layer was used in a PyTorch model?
options: Every hybrid model would require hand-written gradient-plumbing code instead of being able to drop a QNode into a model like any other layer -- exactly the manual work TorchLayer's autograd integration eliminates
Nothing would change; manual interception would be exactly as convenient as automatic integration
The parameter-shift rule itself would no longer be mathematically valid
PyTorch models would become unable to use any classical layers at all
questions.explain: The whole practical value of TorchLayer's autograd integration is removing the need to hand-write the hybrid loop from Lesson 19 every time -- manual backward-pass interception would reintroduce exactly that burden for every hybrid model built.
